the result of a multiplication
the result of a division
an approximate answer to check against

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Number
lessons.title: Divisibility rules
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you tell if 3 744 is divisible by 9 without dividing?
objectives: Know and use divisibility rules for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10
Use divisibility to find factors quickly
Explain why a divisibility rule works
successCriteria: Use the rules for 2, 3, 5 and 10
Use the rules for 4, 6, 8 and 9
Explain why the digit-sum rule works for 3 and 9
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: checking codes such as ISBNs; History: number systems
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order and patterns in numbers

keywords.def: can be divided exactly with no remainder
the total of a number's digits
a number that divides exactly into another
a reliable test that always works

teach.heading: The rules
teach.note: Go through the table and test each with 3 744.

teach.heading: Testing a big number
bullets: Write yes or no with a reason
teach.note: Model all the tests.

model.problem: Is 3 744 divisible by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9?
steps: By 2 and 3, so by 6: yes; 744 = 8 × 93: by 8, yes

teach.heading: Why the digit sum works
teach.note: Higher attainers love this. Show that the multiples of 9 vanish, leaving the digit sum. That is why it works for 3 and 9 only.

teach.heading: The rule for 6
teach.note: Ask: 'Does 'divisible by 3 and 4' mean divisible by 12?' Yes, because 3 and 4 share no factors. But '2 and 4' does not mean 8.

misconception.wrong: Divisible by 2 and 4, so divisible by 8 (e.g. 12)
misconception.right: Combine only when the numbers share no factor: 2 and 3 → 6

teach.heading: Check: divisibility
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.why: 4 + 5 + 1 + 8 = 18, which is divisible by 9. The other digit sums are 10, 10 and 16, none divisible by 9.

practice: Find a digit to make 47□ divisible by 6
independent: Core: Test 5 040 for divisibility by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10
Extend: Find the smallest 4-digit number divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

exit: Why is 135 divisible by 5 but not by 10?

lessons.send: Support: rules card. Stretch: research the rule for 11.

lessons.title: Powers and roots
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is 'squared' called squared and 'cubed' called cubed?
objectives: To understand how squares, cubes and their roots are linked as inverse operations
successCriteria: All: recall square numbers to 15² and cube numbers to 5³
Most: find square roots and cube roots, including negative square roots

keywords.def: a number times itself, such as 7² = 49
a number times itself three times, such as 4³ = 64
the number that squares to make it: √49 = 7
the number that cubes to make it: ∛64 = 4
the opposite operation

hook.text: A square garden has an area of 50 m². Is its side more or less than 7 m? How could you tell without a calculator?
hook.a: More than 7 m: 7² = 49 is just under 50, so the side is a little over 7 m.

teach.heading: Why 'squared'?
bullets: 7² is the area of a 7 by 7 square
4³ is the volume of a 4 by 4 by 4 cube
teach.note: Show the square and cube pictures; the names come from shapes.

teach.heading: Learn these
teach.note: Pupils test each other in breakout pairs.

teach.heading: Roots undo powers
bullets: 81 also has a negative square root: -9
teach.note: (-9)² = 81 too, so x² = 81 has two solutions.

teach.heading: Estimating √50
teach.note: √50 is just over 7 (about 7.07).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: (-2)³ = -8, so ∛-8 = -2. A cube root of a negative number exists; a square root of a negative does not (in real numbers).

practice.q: Between which two whole numbers is √90?

independent.q: Extend: Estimate √130 to 1 decimal place, then check with a calculator.
Stretch: A cube has a volume of 343 cm³. Find the area of one face.

exit.q: What is √121?
Between which two whole numbers is ∛30?
Big question: why is 4³ called '4 cubed'?
exit.a: It is the volume of a cube with edges of 4 units.

lessons.send: Support: squares and cubes table. EAL: 'square', 'cube', 'root'. Stretch: estimate √200 to 1 d.p. without a calculator.

teach.heading: Model

writing a number as a product of prime factors

The image is 2 to the left of x = 3

teach.heading: Which line?
teach.note: Pupils draw it.

misconception.wrong: Reflecting in x = 3 means reflecting in the x-axis
misconception.right: x = 3 is the vertical line through 3 on the x-axis

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.why: The x-axis is horizontal: x stays, y changes sign. (-2, 5) is the reflection in the y-axis.

practice.q: Reflect (-3, 4) in the y-axis and in the x-axis.
practice.model:
y-axis: x changes sign, (3, 4).
x-axis: y changes sign, (-3, -4).

independent.q: Core (printable grid): Triangle T has vertices (1, 2), (3, 2) and (3, 5). Reflect T in (a) the y-axis (b) the x-axis (c) x = 4 (d) y = 1. Write each image's coordinates.
independent.model:
(a) Each x changes sign: (1, 2) goes to (-1, 2), and so on.
(c) (1, 2) is 3 left of x = 4, so its image is 3 right: (7, 2).

independent.q: Extend: A shape is reflected in x = 2 and one image vertex is (-1, 4). Where was the original vertex?
Stretch: Reflect (a, b) in the line x = k. Write the image in terms of a, b and k.

exit.q: Reflect (4, -3) in the y-axis:
Is the image congruent to the object?
Big question: where does a reflected shape go, and what stays the same?
exit.a: The same distance to the other side of the mirror line; size, shape and angles stay the same, but it is flipped.

lessons.bigQuestion: How can you find the mirror line when you only see the object and its image?

successCriteria: All: reflect a point or shape in y = x by swapping the coordinates

keywords.def: the diagonal line through (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)
the line a shape is reflected in
name the transformation and give its mirror line as an equation
a point that does not move

hook.text: The point (2, 5) is reflected and lands on (5, 2). Where is the mirror line? What happened to the coordinates?
hook.a: The line y = x; the coordinates swapped.

teach.heading: Four mirror lines
teach.note: Pupils test each rule on (2, 5).

teach.heading: Reflect in y = x
teach.note: Draw y = x first.

model.problem: Reflect the triangle (1, 3), (2, 6), (4, 3) in the line y = x.

teach.heading: Describing a reflection
teach.note: The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each object-image pair.

model.problem: (1, 2), (3, 2), (3, 4) maps to (1, -4), (3, -4), (3, -6). Describe the transformation fully.

teach.heading: Full description
bullets: Name it and give the equation
teach.note: Exam mark schemes need both.

misconception.right: Write 'reflection in the line y = -1': the transformation and the mirror line's equation

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Reflect (3, -1) in the line y = x:
check.why: Swap the coordinates: (-1, 3). (1, -3) also changes the signs, which is the rule for y = -x.

practice.q: Reflect (4, 7) in y = x and in y = -x.
practice.model:
y = x: swap, (7, 4).
y = -x: swap and change both signs, (-7, -4).

independent.q: Core: (a) Reflect the triangle (1, 1), (4, 1), (1, 2) in y = x. (b) Reflect it in y = -x. (c) Describe fully: (2, 3), (5, 3), (5, 4) maps to (2, -1), (5, -1), (5, -2). (d) Describe fully: (0, 1), (2, 1), (2, 4) maps to (6, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4).
independent.model:
(a) Swap each pair: (1, 1) stays (it is on the line), (4, 1) → (1, 4), (1, 2) → (2, 1).
(c) Midpoint of y = 3 and y = -1 is y = 1; check the others: 4 and -2 also give 1.

independent.q: Extend: Which points do not move when reflected in y = x?
independent.a: Every point on the line y = x, such as (3, 3): they are invariant

independent.q: Stretch: Reflect (2, 5) in the x-axis, then reflect the result in the y-axis. What single transformation does the same?
independent.a: (-2, -5): a rotation of 180° about the origin

exit.q: Reflect (6, 1) in y = x:
Object (0, 2), image (0, -6). Mirror line?
Big question: how do you find the mirror line from an object and its image?
exit.a: Find the midpoints of each point and its image; the mirror line passes through them all (the perpendicular bisector).
